TENTATIVE RULINGS FOR Feb.24, 2026
Department R17 - Judge Gilbert G. Ochoa

ANDREW AUBEL
v.

GENERAL MOTORS, LLC
CIVRS2400910
Motion: Attorney Fees, Costs, and Expenses
Movant: Plaintiff Andrew Aubel
Respondent: Defendant General Motors, LLC
Discussion
Statement of the Law. In general, attorney fees, costs, and expenses are recoverable
under the Song-Beverly Act. Civil Code section 1794, subdivision (d) provides:
If the buyer prevails in an action under this section, the buyer shall
be allowed by the court to recover as part of the judgment a sum
equal to the aggregate amount of costs and expenses, including
attorney's fees based on actual time expended, determined by the
court to have been reasonably incurred by the buyer in connection
with the commencement and prosecution of such action.
To prevail under the Act, the buyer must have recovered damages and/or other legal/equitable
relief. (Civ. Code § 1794, subd. (a).)
In determining the reasonableness of the fees, the court applies the lodestar method, i.e.,
multiplying the number of hours reasonably worked by a reasonable hourly rate. (Flannery v.
Prentice (2001) 26 Cal.4th 572, 584.) The Court can reduce hours that appear unreasonably
inflated. (Chavez v. City of Los Angeles (2010) 47 Cal.4th 970, 990.) Additionally, inefficient or
duplicative efforts are not subject to compensation. (Premier Medical Management Systems, Inc.
v. California Ins. Guarantee Ass’n (2008) 163 Cal.App.4th 550, 556.)
The burden is on the party seeking attorney fees to prove that the fees it seeks are
reasonable. (Center for Biological Diversity v. County of San Bernardino (2010) 188
Cal.App.4th 603, 615.) “[Parties] are not entitled to compensation for this work merely because
it was performed. It [is] their burden to persuade the trial court the work was reasonably
necessary, both as to the particular tasks performed and the amount of time devoted to them.”
(Baxter v. Bock (2016) 247 Cal.App.4th 775, 793.)
Reasonable Hours. The starting point for every fee award is calculating an attorney’s
services in terms of time expanded on the case. (Levy v. Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc. (1992)
4 Cal.App.4th 807, 815.)
In reaching the lodestar, a court begins by deciding “the reasonable hours spent” on the
case and multiplying that number by “the hourly prevailing rate for private attorneys in the
community conducting noncontingent litigation of the same type.” (Ketchum v. Moses (2001) 24
Cal.4th 1122, 1133 (Ketchum).) “[T]he unadorned lodestar reflects the general local hourly rate
for a fee-bearing case; it does not include any compensation for contingent risk, extraordinary
skill, or any other factors a trial court may consider under Serrano III.” (Id. at p. 1138
[discussing Serrano v. Priest (1977) 20 Cal.3d 25 (Serrano).].)
Reasonable Hourly Rate. Requested rates are reasonable if they are “within the range of
reasonable rates charged by and judicially awarded comparable attorneys for comparable work.”
(Children’s Hosp. & Med. Ctr. v. Bontá (2002) 97 Cal.App.4th 740, 783.)
A reasonable hourly rate is one that is prevailing in the community where the case is
litigated for similar work. (MBNA America Bank, N.A. v. Gorman (2006) 147 Cal.App.4th Supp.
1, 13.)
Analysis. Plaintiff moves for an award of attorney fees as the prevailing party in this
action in light of the parties’ settlement agreement. Plaintiff seeks fees in the amount of
$31,042.50 plus $3,104.25 (.1 multiplier) and $1,477.15 in costs, for a total of $35,623.90.
Reasonable Hours. In support of the motion, counsel for Plaintiff, David N. Barry
submits a declaration. He attests that prior to initiating litigation, Plaintiff contacted GM, who
refused to repurchase or replace the vehicle. (Barry Decl. ¶ 7.) Plaintiff retained counsel and suit
was filed on September 13, 2024. (¶ 9.) Plaintiff then commenced discovery by filing the
Complaint, noticing the depositions of GM’S Person(s) Most Knowledgeable, employees
involved in GM’s investigation of Plaintiff’s prelitigation repurchase demand, propounding
written discovery, and meeting and conferring with GM’S counsel regarding various litigation
tasks and court requirements. (¶ 10.) GM opposed Plaintiff’s Motion to Compel and filed an
Answer rather than settle the claims. (¶¶ 11-12.) Between September 2024 and December 2024,
Plaintiff engaged in extensive meet and confer efforts with GM hoping to informally resolve the
discovery disputes and settle. (¶ 13.) Attorney Barry notes that the discovery motions filed in this
matter would not have been necessary had GM provided code compliant responses. (¶ 14.) Then,
after filing an Opposition, on April 15, 2025, GM offered to settle the matter for $106,000, and
Plaintiff accepted this—the first section 998 offer made. (¶ 15; Exh. 3.) Attorney Barry himself
handled the negotiations for settlement and attempted to informally resolve the issue of attorney
fees. (¶ 16.) Barry attests all time entries were completed contemporaneously and set forth the
actual time expended on matters. He reviewed the billing records and removed de miminis fees.
He also does not bill for support staff, secretarial, or paralegal time. (¶ 18.) The billing records
are attached as Exhibit 4 to the declaration. (¶ 19; Exh. 4.)
GM opposes the motion and argues that a reasonable fee award in this matter is
$11,827.50 in fees and $1,031 in costs. GM argues the fee award sought includes substantial
inefficiencies, duplicative efforts, and extensive reliance on templates.
Templates. GM takes issue with specific entries. For example, with respect to the use of
templates, GM flags entries on November 21 and 25, 2024, totaling 3.2 hours billed by Ms.
Quinn, to draft discovery requests and deposition notices. GM also takes issue with entries made
on November 21, 22, 26, 27 and December 20, 23, and 24 for preparing template discovery
responses consisting of 4.4 hours of work. GM also flags entries for January 6, February 21, 25,
25, April 17, 21, 29, May 8, and June 3, 2025 for templated Motions to Compel where Ms.
Quinn billed a total of 19.6 hours to draft what GM calls four unnecessary motions to compel
that were eventually withdrawn.

Here, it appears as if GM has miscalculated the billing entries. The November 21 and 24,
2025 hours do not total 3.2 but rather 1.5 hours. Regardless, the Court DENIES GM’s request
for reductions here. The hours billed across the number of motions and tasks are not
unreasonable and already appear to account for the fact that counsel is using templates and not
drafting anew.

Discovery Review. Meanwhile, GM takes issue with 3.3 hours billed on December 6, 19,
and 20, 2024, January 20, 2025, by Ms. Quinn to review GM’s discovery responses (including
objections, responses, and document production). GM argues 1 hour was sufficient time. The
Court DENIES this request. Discovery in lemon law matters can be voluminous, and the 3.3
hours is reasonable and already reflects the repetitive nature of these types of cases.
Meet and Confer correspondence. GM takes issue with two entries from December 9 and
27, 2024 consisting of 3.3 hours billed to draft meet and confer correspondence. However, GM
ignores the fact that this was not a quick meet and confer letter but detailed on December 9 as
consisting of 10 pages and the December 27 letter consisting of 40 pages. Proofreading alone
could cover the time billed. GM’s counsel, Matthew Dobson submits a declaration with exhibits
attached to show only the names and other information changes; however, counsel still needs to
read the documents to ensure what needs editing and to make the appropriate changes. The
amount of time billed, in light of that, is reasonable.The Court DENIES the request to reduce the
time billed here.

Fee Motion. The Barry Law Firm seeks 9.4 hours for the fee motion, which GM claims is
excessive. GM argues this should be reduced by 5.4 hours. The Courdenies the request to reduce
the hours. Upon review, their hours are reasonable. Plaintiff seeks these hours for drafting the
motion, the proposed Order, the memorandum of costs, to review and revise it, to review the
Opposition, to draft a reply, and to prepare for and attend the hearing. The total time is not
unreasonable to complete these tasks.

In sum, the Court finds that all hours billed were reasonable.
Reasonable Hourly Rates. “To enable the trial court to determine whether attorney fees
should be awarded and in what amount, an attorney should present ‘(1) evidence, documentary
and oral, of the services actually performed; and (2) expert opinion, by [the applicant] and other
lawyers, as to what would be a reasonable fee for such services.’” (Martino v. Denevi (1986) 182
Cal.App.3d 553, 558-559.) “Testimony of an attorney as to the number of hours worked on a
particular case is sufficient evidence to support an award of attorney fees, even in the absence of
detailed time records.” (Ibid.)
To substantiate his firm’s hourly rates, Attorney Barry attaches the United States
Consumer Law Fee Survey Report for the 2017-2018 year to his declaration. (Barry Decl. ¶ 20;
Exh. 5.) He also attaches a national survey, including California, concerning the fees of
consumer law attorneys. (¶ 22; Exh. 7.)
Barry attests he is aware of the hourly rates of other attorneys in California who work in
the area of lemon law and consumer law. An hourly rate of $675.00 per hour for himself, he
attests, is consistent with other attorneys who litigate consumer matters and who have his level of
experience. He is counsel of record and lead counsel for Plaintiff. He routinely charges $675 per
hour, which is routinely paid in most consumer claims that he has resolved. (¶ 23.) He has been
practicing law for almost 23 years and for nearly 20 of those, he has practiced consumer law. He
has operated his own firm since August 2010. He has tried 14 jury trials to verdict and handled
numerous binding arbitrations. (¶ 24.) He graduated from Pepperdine School of Law in 2000,
was a member of the law review, and was admitted to the New York State Bar in 2004. (¶¶ 25-
26.) Barry also provides a list of cases in which his hourly rate has been approved. (¶¶ 28-78.)
This includes cases from San Bernardino County and this Court. (See e.g., Barry Decl. ¶¶ 60, 61,
and 65.)
Attorney Elizabeth Quinn also submits a declaration. She has been an attorney for 25
years, specializing in consumer protection having received her law degree from Pepperdine in
2000. (Quinn Decl. ¶¶ 1, 5.) She attests to the correctness of her billing entries. (¶ 3.) She
previously practiced as a trial attorney, senior associate, and manager of civil litigation at other
firms. She was a sole practitioner from May 2008 until May 2018. (¶¶ 8-10.) She has been with
the Barry Law Firm since August 2018, and her rate is $600/hour. (¶ 11.) Her fee has been
approved in a number of cases, which she lists. (See Quinn Decl. ¶¶ 12-35.)
GM does not oppose the rates charged by Barry or Quinn.
Multiplier. Plaintiff seeks a .1 multiplier because the case was taken on a contingency
basis. Throughout the motion, Plaintiff also claims the result was exceptional. However, Plaintiff
is also not asking for historical rates but current rates throughout the motion and is thus
requesting a multiplier on top of a multiplier.
Once the lodestar figure is calculated it “may be adjusted by the court based on factors
including ... (1) the novelty and difficulty of the questions involved, (2) the skill displayed in
presenting them, (3) the extent to which the nature of the litigation precluded other employment
by the attorneys, and (4) the contingent nature of the fee award.” (Serrano, supra, 20 Cal.3d at p.
40.) “The purpose of such adjustment is to fix a fee at the fair market value for the particular
action. In effect, the court determines, retrospectively, whether the litigation involved a
contingent risk or required extraordinary legal skill justifying augmentation of the unadorned
lodestar in order to approximate the fair market rate for such services.” (Ketchum, supra, 24
Cal.4th at p. 1132.)
Here, the Court DENIES the multiplier. While the case was taken on a contingency, this
alone does not warrant a multiplier. The case also appears fairly routine.
Costs. Plaintiff seeks $1,477.15 in costs.
“Except as otherwise expressly provided by statute, a prevailing party is entitled as a
matter of right to recover costs in any action or proceeding.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 1032, subd. (b).)
Absent statutory authority, the Court has no discretion to deny costs to the prevailing party.
(Nelson v. Anderson (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 111, 129 (Nelson).)
The losing party may dispute any or all of the items in the prevailing party’s costs bill by
a motion to strike or tax costs. (See Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1700(b).) Technically, a motion to
strike challenges the entire costs bill (e.g., on the ground the claimant is not the “prevailing
party”), whereas a motion to tax challenges particular items or amounts. But the terms are often
used interchangeably and there is no difference in the procedural rules. (Ibid., rule 3.1700(b)(2).)
Costs statutes are to be strictly construed. (See Sequoia Vacuum Systems v. Stransky
(1964) 229 Cal.App.2d 281, 289.) Code of Civil Procedure section 1033.5 sets forth allowable
costs and costs that are not allowable; furthermore, section 1033.5, subdivision (c), paragraph (2)
restricts allowable costs to those reasonably necessary to the conduct of the litigation. In
addition, under Code of Civil Procedure section 1033.5, subdivision (c), paragraph (4), items not
mentioned in section 1033.5 may be allowed or denied in the discretion of the Court. The
allowable and not allowable costs are determined by Code of Civil Procedure section 1033.5,
subdivision (a) and (b).

Pursuant to section 1033.5, subdivision (a), items allowable as costs include filing and
motion fees, deposition costs, service of process fess, attorney fees when authorized by contract
or statute, court reporter fees, and fees for models and blowups of exhibits that are reasonably
helpful to the trier of fact. Allowable costs are awarded if: (1) incurred, whether or not paid; (2)
reasonably necessary to the conduct of the litigation rather than merely convenient or beneficial
to its preparation; and (3) reasonable in amount. (Code Civ. Proc. § 1033.5, subd. (c).) Thus,
even costs allowable as a matter of right may be disallowed if not reasonably necessary or not
reasonable in amount. (Perko’s Enterprises, Inc. v. RRNS Enterprises (1992) 4 Cal.App.4th 238,
245.)
If the items appearing on a costs bill appear to be proper charges, the verified
memorandum is prima facie evidence that the costs are proper and the party seeking to tax costs
bears the burden of showing they are not reasonable or necessary. If the items are properly
objected to, however, then the party seeking costs bears the burden. (Nelson, supra, 72
Cal.App.4th at p. 131.) The mere filing of a motion to tax costs may be a “proper objection” to
an item, the necessity of which appears doubtful, or which does not appear to be proper on its
face. (Ibid. [citing Oak Grove School Dist. v. City Title Ins. Co. (1963) 217 Cal.App.2d 678, 698-
699].) However, where costs are not expressly allowed by the statute, the burden is on the party
claiming the costs to show that the charges were reasonable and necessary. (Ibid.) Where the
objections are based on factual matters, the motion to tax or strike must be supported by
evidence. (County of Kern v. Ginn (1983) 146 Cal.App.3d 1107, 1113-1114.)
Whether an item listed on the costs bill was reasonably necessary is a question of fact for
the trial court, whose decision is reviewed on appeal for abuse of discretion. (Bender v. County
of Los Angeles (2013) 217 Cal.App.4th 968, 989.)
Analysis. GM takes issue Costs for Numbers 1, 12, and 14. First, GM challenges the
filing and motion fees. GM argues that the four discovery motions were ultimately withdrawn;
however, this does not then render then unreasonable. The filing of the motions may have
contributed to the timing of GM’s decision to settle.
Next, GM challenges the court reporter fees, which are yet to occur. So long as a court
reporter is present for the fee motion, the Court awards these costs.
Finally, GM argues that counsel improperly seeks $150.95 for electronic filing or service
without an explanation as to what this is for. With the Reply, there is no clarification as to what
these costs were incurred for. Therefore, as GM raised a valid objection, the Court reduces the
costs by $150.95.

Ruling
The Court GRANTS the motion in part and award attorney fees in the amount of
$31,042.50 and costs in the amount of $1,326.20 (provided there is a court reporter at the fee
motion hearing), for a total award of $32,368.70.
Movant to give Notice and prepare Order.

Dated:

Judge Gilbert G. Ochoa
TENTATIVE RULINGS FOR Feb.24, 2026
Department R17 - Judge Gilbert G. Ochoa

YOUNG SU KIM
V.

JIN W. KIM, aka JIN KIM
CIVRS2401616
Motion: Motion for Reconsideration
Movant: Plaintiff Young Su Kim
Respondent: Defendant Jin W. Kim
New or Different Facts, Circumstances, or Law
Plaintiff argues that the Set Aside Order should be overturned because on October 16,
2025, just six (6) days before the Court’s Set Aside Order was entered, Defendant appeared
remotely at a hearing, in pro per and without a translator, in a separate lawsuit filed by Plaintiff
against Defendant in Orange County Superior Court, Case No. 30-2025-01458509-CU-CD-CJC
(“OC Action”). (Muriella Decl. ¶ 9.) Plaintiff argues that this contradicts Defendant’s prior
testimony made in his declaration in support of his Set Aside Motion that Defendant was
completely unfamiliar with the legal process and that he was somehow incapable of understanding
what was required of him when served with legal process.
As is relevant to this Motion, Defendant originally made the following statements in his
initial declaration attached to the Set Aside Motion.
2. In or around late 2024, I was served with documents, that I later came to
understand were legal documents related to this case. Although I now understand
these were the Complaint and Summons, at the time I received them, I did not
comprehend what they were or what they required me to do. Due to my very limited
understanding of the legal process, I did not realize that I was required to take legal
action or respond within a certain timeframe. As a result, I inadvertently did not
immediately contact a lawyer or otherwise take steps to respond to the lawsuit.
3. I did not willfully ignore or avoid these legal documents. I simply did not
understand their nature or the consequences of not responding. I now understand
the seriousness of the matter and deeply regret not having sought help sooner.
4. I retained my current counsel on March 25, 2025. Although I delayed slightly in
seeking counsel and filing my responsive pleading, I first became aware that
something serious had happened when I was informed by my attorney in April 2025
that my answer had been rejected and a default had been entered against me.
(J. Kim Decl iso Set Aside Mtn, ¶¶ 2-4.)
In opposition to the Set Aside Motion, Plaintiff testified that he is personally familiar with
Defendant because Defendant is Plaintiff’s step-son and further testified that Defendant is fluent
in English. (Y. Kim Decl iso Opp. to Set Aside Mtn, ¶ 6.) Given this, the parties essentially
disagreed about whether it was reasonable to conclude that Defendant was incapable of
understanding the legal process.

On August 14, 2025, the Court allowed the Plaintiff to take a limited-scope deposition of
Defendant as to the issues raised in the Set Aside Motion pleadings and further allowed the Parties
to submit supplemental declarations. (See 08/14/2025 Minute Order.)
Following this, on September 2, 2025, Defendant submitted a supplemental declaration
admitting that he is able to speak English, but that he did not have any experience with legal
proceedings at the time Defendant was served with a copy of the Summons and Complaint.
Defendant further testified that he had welcomed his first child on November 10, 2025, before he
had been served with legal process, and that following his child’s birth, Defendant had taken on a
majority of the baby care responsibilities, which were made more difficult by the fact that the
newborn had severe eczema and jaundice, and because his wife had limited mobility due to
undergoing a cesarean section. Defendant testified that between his family circumstances and his
limited understanding of the legal process, he was unable to timely address these proceedings.
(Supp. J. Kim Decl iso Set Aside Mtn, ¶¶ 3-8.)
On September 29, 2025, Plaintiff also submitted a supplemental declaration, in which he
attached copies of Defendant’s Answer and a Case Management Statement (“CMS”) filed on April
9, 2025, and on July 2, 2025, respectively, in the OC Action. (Supp. Y. Kim Decl iso Opp. to Set
Aside Mtn, ¶¶ 4-5, Exhs. 1-2.)
In opposition, Defendant argues that the controverted issue of whether Defendant was
unfamiliar with the legal process is not a “new” fact and points out that the Court allowed the
parties to file supplemental briefing on this issue and also allowed Plaintiff to conduct a limited-
scope deposition of Defendant on this very same issue. Defendant also argues that the “fact” that
Defendant attended a hearing in the OC Action without a translator or attorney present is
unsubstantiated because Plaintiff fails to provide any competent evidence or foundation.
When the evidence is considered, Defendant’s argument that the fact that Plaintiff’s “new”
evidence is unsubstantiated is unpersuasive. In support of the Motion, Plaintiff submits the
declaration of his attorney, Sam M. Muriella, who testifies that he was personally present at the
hearing at issue in the OC Action. (See Muriella Decl. ¶ 9.) As such, Muriella was a percipient
witness and would therefore be squarely competent to testify to things he heard and saw on that
day of the hearing in the OC Action.

Nevertheless, it does not appear that Plaintiff’s “new” evidence justifies reconsideration.
Here, as admitted by Plaintiff, Defendant appeared at the hearing in the OC Action on October 16,
2025. By that time, more than five (5) months had already passed since Defendant filed the Set
Aside Motion on May 1, 2025. Notably, Defendant had never testified that he is incapable of
understanding the English language, and instead, had repeatedly testified that he was simply
unfamiliar with the legal process at the time he was served with legal process in late 2024. (J. Kim
Decl iso Set Aside Mtn, ¶¶ 2-3; Supp. J. Kim Decl iso Set Aside Mtn, ¶¶ 3-8.) Defendant also
testified that he later learned of the legal requirements when he retained an attorney in April 2025.
(See J. Kim Decl iso Set Aside Mtn, ¶ 4.) Therefore, it is not surprising that after becoming more
familiar with the legal process, Defendant was able to attend the hearing in the OC Action on
October 16, 2025. In the exact same vein, Defendant’s line of testimony also does not pose
contradictions to the fact that Defendant had filed his Answer and CMS on April 9, 2025, and on
July 2, 2025, respectively, in the OC Action.

In making the Court’s Set Aside Order, the Court noted that there was only a three-month
delay between entry of default and the filing of the Set Aside Motion, and that there is a strong
public policy in favor of granting relief and allowing the requesting party his or her day in court
in the absence of prejudice suffered by Plaintiff. (Rappleyea v. Campbell (1994) 8 Cal.4th 975,
980, 981.) To the extent that Plaintiff argues that the Court’s ruling is erroneous because he asserts
that the Court misinterpreted the law, or alternatively, because it misinterpreted the evidence, these
are not a proper bases for a reconsideration motion. Reconsideration cannot be granted based on
claims the court misinterpreted the law or facts in its initial ruling. That is not a “new” or
“different” matter justifying reconsideration of the Court’s prior ruling. (Gilberd, supra, 32
Cal.App.4th at p. 1500.)
Ruling
Therefore, the Court DENIES Plaintiff’s Motion for Reconsideration of the Set Aside
Order.

Movant to give Notice and prepare Order.

Judge Gilbert G. Ochoa
TENTATIVE RULINGS FOR Feb.24, 2026
Department R17 - Judge Gilbert G. Ochoa

KIMBERLY STOCKWELL
V.

TARGET CORPORATION, ET AL.

CIVRS2504927
Motion: Quash Deposition Subpoena (x2)
Movant: Plaintiff Kimberly Stockwell
Respondent: Defendant Target Corporation

DISCUSSION
I. Legal Standard
Code of Civil Procedure section 1987.1, subdivision (a), states:
If a subpoena requires the attendance of a witness or the production of books,
documents, electronically stored information, or other things before a court, or at
the trial of an issue therein, or at the taking of a deposition, the court, upon motion
reasonably made by any person described in subdivision (b), or upon the court's
own motion after giving counsel notice and an opportunity to be heard, may make
an order quashing the subpoena entirely, modifying it, or directing compliance with
it upon those terms or conditions as the court shall declare, including protective
orders. In addition, the court may make any other order as may be appropriate to
protect the person from unreasonable or oppressive demands, including
unreasonable violations of the right of privacy of the person.
A party, witness, consumer, employee, or person whose personal identifying information
is sought may bring a motion to quash. (Code of Civ. Proc., § 1987.1, subd. (b).) No meet and
confer effort is required to bring a motion to quash. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1987.1.) If a party seeks
to subpoena personal records, then the party must serve the consumer a notice along with a copy
of the subpoena. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1985.3, subd. (b) and (e).) The party-consumer whose records
are sought may move to quash or modify the subpoena under Code of Civil Procedure section
1987.1. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1985.3, subd. (g).) Five days before production, the deposition officer
and witness are to be notified of the motion. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1985.3, subd. (g).)
Sanctions against the losing party are discretionary, pursuant to Section 1987.2, if the court
finds the motion was made or opposed in bad faith or without substantial justification, or if one or
more of the requirements of the subpoena was oppressive. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1987.2.) When a
trial court exercises its discretion to issue discovery sanctions, the court must delineate the specific
acts upon which the sanctions are awarded. (First City Properties, Inc. v. MacAdam (1996) 49
Cal.App.4th 507, 515.)
II. Analysis
A. Timeliness
Under Code of Civil Procedure sections 1985.3, subdivision (g) and 1985.6, subdivision
(f)(1), a motion to quash by a “consumer” or an “employee” must be served on the witness and the
deposition officer at least five days before the date set for production of the subpoenaed records.
In opposition, Target argues that Plaintiff’s BBW Motion is untimely because the BBW
Subpoena and associated Notices to Consumer or Employee and Objection were served on
September 4, 2025, and required BBW to produce its documents by September 29, 2025. Thus,
Plaintiff’s deadline to file the Motion to Quash was September 24, 2025. (Durcharme Decl. iso
BBW Motion, ¶ 6, Exh. E.)
Although Plaintiff attempted to serve a copy of the BBW Motion and all supporting
documents on September 24, 2025, Target asserts that the Notice of Motion did not contain any
hearing date or time. Ultimately, Plaintiff did not properly notice or file the BBW Motion until the
next day, on September 25, 2025. (Durcharme Decl. iso BBW Motion, ¶¶ 10-11, Exhs. H, I.) As
such, Target argues that the BBW Motion is untimely because it was not properly noticed or filed
before the five-day deadline.

However, the five-day time limit for service is not jurisdictional. The court can grant a
motion to quash service even after the date set for production. (Slagle v. Superior Court (1989)
211 Cal.App.3d 1309, 1312-1313.) The time limits for bringing a motion to quash are simply
designed to guide those involved as to when the witness with the records may safely honor or not
honor the subpoena when the consumer objects. (Id. at p. 1312.)
Here, given that Target did not identify that it suffered any prejudice from the delay and
because Target admits that it was fully aware that Plaintiff would be seeking to file a Motion to
Quash since at least September 9, 2025, the Court to rules on the merits of the BBW Motion.
B. Meet and Confer/IDC
Target also argues that both Motions should be denied because Plaintiff failed to meet and
confer in good faith and also failed to schedule an IDC before filing either Motion.
Here, Plaintiff served her objections to the BBW Subpoena on September 9, 2025 and to
the PBO Subpoena on September 30, 2025. (Durcharme Decl. iso BBW/PBO Motion, ¶ 7, Exh.
F.)
In regard to the BBW Subpoena, Target states that Plaintiff did not request to meet and
confer with Target until September 24, 2025 at 9:49 a.m., but only provided Target with less than
3 hours’ time to respond by 12:00 p.m. Although Target responded on the same day and requested
a call, Plaintiff’s Counsel refused to discuss the matter and told Target that she intended to file a
Motion to Quash. (Durcharme Decl. iso BBW Motion, ¶ 9, Exh. G.)
In regard to the PBO Subpoena, Target states that it sent a letter aiming to address
Plaintiff’s objections to the PBO Subpoena and stated that it remained open to discussing the scope
of both Subpoenas on October 7, 2025. However, Plaintiff did not respond to this letter and filed
the PBO Motion on October 15, 2025. (Durcharme Decl. iso PBO Motion, ¶ 8, Exh. G.)
However, contrary to Target’s assertations, there is nothing in Code of Civil Procedure
section 1985.3, subdivision (g), or alternatively, section 1985.6, subdivision (f)(4), that requires a
moving party to meet and confer before filing a motion to quash. Furthermore, on reply, Plaintiff
points out that it is undisputed that Plaintiff, had on two occasions, requested a 14-day extension
on September 23, 2025 and on September 24, 2025 to engage in substantive meet and confer
conversations. (See Durcharme Decl. iso BBW Motion, ¶ 8, Exh. G; Supp. Davtyan Decl. Exhs.
1-2.) However, without Target’s simultaneous agreement to extend the deadline on the filing of
the Motion to Quash, Plaintiff was forced to file the Motions.
When the evidence is considered, it appears that Plaintiff was indeed tardy in taking the
first steps towards engaging in meet and confer efforts, but that Target also did not act in good
faith manner in meeting and conferring with Plaintiff as it refused to stipulate to an extension of
time to meet and confer. Nonetheless, because meeting and conferring is not a prerequisite to filing
a motion to quash, there are no grounds for denying the instant Motions on this basis.
As for Target’s IDC argument, this is also unpersuasive because the Court did not enter
the IDC Order in this Action until December 22, 2025, which was at least two months after both
Motions had already been filed.

C. Merits of Motion
Target’s Subpoenas seeks all records in BBW and PBO’s custody, possession, and control
relating to Plaintiff’s employment with each respective employer, i.e., from May 1, 2019 to June
30, 2019 for BBW and from July 1, 2014 to June 30, 2019 for PBO. Both Subpoenas requires
BBW and PBO to produce the following documents:
1. All job applications completed by Plaintiff;
2. All resumes, cover letters, and other documents submitted by Plaintiff in seeking
employment with BWE or PBO;
3. All interview notes, summaries, and other documents describing the information
discussed during Plaintiff’s job interview(s) for employment with BWE or PBO;
4. All offer letters, employment agreements/contracts, and other documents showing
Plaintiff’s pay rate and entitlement to employee benefits;
5. The job description for each position Plaintiff held during her employment with BWE
or PBO;
6. Any and all documents regarding Plaintiff’s job duties during her employment with
BWE or PBO;
7. Any and all documents regarding Plaintiff’s performance during her employment with
BWE or PBO;
8. All disciplinary records for misconduct relating to Plaintiff;
9. Any and all documents regarding any complaints Plaintiff made during her
employment with BWE or PBO;
10. All documents reflecting compensation paid to Plaintiff; and
11. If applicable, all documents related to the end of Plaintiff’s employment, including but
not limited to documents showing the reason Plaintiff’s employment ended, separation
agreements, severance agreements, resignation letter(s), exit interview notes, and final
pay records.
(Davtyan Decl. iso BBW/PBO Motion, Exh 1.)
Additionally, the BBW Subpoena also seeks an additional 12th category of documents
consisting of “[a]ny non-privileged documents related to any litigation brought by [Plaintiff]
against BBW that are not available in the public record, including [Plaintiff]’s deposition
transcript, discovery responses, document productions, and the like.” (Davtyan Decl. iso BBW
Motion, Exh 1.)
Plaintiff argues that the Subpoenas violate her right to privacy and that her prior
employment records are irrelevant to the allegations in this FEHA discrimination lawsuit against
Target because character and propensity evidence is not admissible in civil actions under Evidence
Code section 1101.

Discovery is relevant if admissible or likely to lead to admissible evidence. (Code Civ.
Proc., § 2017.010.) “In the context of discovery, evidence is ‘relevant’ if it might reasonably assist
a party in evaluating its case, preparing for trial, or facilitating a settlement.” (Glenfed Dev. Corp.
v. Superior Court (National Union Fire Insurance Company of Pittsburgh, PA) (1997) 53
Cal.App.4th 1113, 1117; Norton v. Superior Court (Ein) (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1750, 1760.)
Individuals have a constitutional right of privacy that protects their information. (Williams
v. Superior Court (Marshalls of CA, LLC) (2017) 3 Cal.5th 531, 552 (Williams).) A privacy interest
is invaded if there is “a legally protected privacy interest, an objectively reasonable expectation of
privacy in the given circumstances, and a threatened intrusion that is serious.” (Ibid.; Hill v.
National Collegiate Athletic Assn (1994) 7 Cal.4th 1, 35-37 (Hill).) However, the constitutional
right to privacy is not absolute. (Palay v. Superior Court (County of Los Angeles) (1993) 18
Cal.App.4th 919, 933.)
When discovery seeks information implicating the constitutional right of privacy, the
standard of review will depend on the seriousness of the invasion, i.e., a compelling interest applies
if the privacy invasion concerns an interest fundamental to personal autonomy but otherwise a
balancing test based on the strength of the privacy interest, the seriousness of the invasion, and the
availability of alternatives and protective measures. (Williams, supra, 3 Cal.5th at p. 552; Lewis v.
Superior Court (Medical Board of California) (2017) 3 Cal.5th 561, 572.)
Under the Hill factors, one’s employment records are shrouded with privacy. (Code of Civ.
Proc., § 1985.6; Marken v. Santa Monica-Malibu Unified School Dist. (2012) 202 Cal.App.4th
1250, 1271; BRV, Inc. v. Superior Court (Dunsmuir Joint Union High School Dist.) (2006) 143
Cal.App.4th 742, 756 [“[E]mployees have a legally protected interest in their personnel files.”].)
Nonetheless, a party waives any privacy interest as to the claims asserted. (Vinson v. Superior
Court (Peralta Community College District) (1987) 43 Cal.3d 833, 842; Britt v. Superior Court
(San Diego Port District) (1978) 20 Cal.3d 844, 863-864 (Britt).)
The party seeking discovery of such private documents must show a particularized need
for the confidential information sought, and the broad “relevancy to the subject matter” standard
is not enough. Instead, the court must be convinced the information is directly relevant to a cause
of action or defense … i.e., that the information is essential to determining the truth of the matters
in dispute. (Britt, supra, 20 Cal.3d at pp. 859-862; Harris v. Superior Court (1992) 3 Cal.App.4th
661, 665, disapproved as noted by Williams, supra, 3 Cal.5th at p. 557, fn. 8.)
In support of Plaintiff’s privacy arguments, Plaintiff cites several out-of-state cases which
hold that the issuance of the subpoenas for an employee’s records creates a profound stigma that
would have a negative on an employee’s future employment prospects. (See Bickley v. Schneider
Nat’l, Inc. (N.D.Cal. 2011) 2011 U.S.Dist.LEXIS 40674, at *9; Guercia v. Equinox Holdings, Inc.
(S.D.N.Y. 2013) 2013 U.S.Dist.LEXIS 71215, at *10.; Salas v. 3M Co. (N.D.Ill. 2008) 2008
U.S.Dist.LEXIS 124993, at *3-4.)
In opposition, Target argues that Plaintiff’s employment records from BBW and PBO are
directly relevant and essential to a fair determination of this Action because those records are at
issue under Target’s Seventh and Twelfth Affirmative Defenses for Unclean Hands and “After-
Acquired Evidence.”
“The doctrine of after-acquired evidence refers to an employer’s discovery, after an
allegedly wrongful termination of employment or refusal to hire, of information that would have
justified a lawful termination or refusal to hire.” (Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co. (2014) 59 Cal.4th
407, 428, emphasis in original (finding after-acquired evidence does not operate as a complete
defense to wrongful acts in violation of the FEHA, as this would “eviscerate the public policies
embodied in the FEHA by allowing an employer to engage in invidious employment
discrimination with total impunity”).) The doctrine of after-acquired evidence applies only where
the employee’s misconduct was “of such severity that the employee in fact would have been
terminated on those grounds alone if the employer had known of it at the time of the discharge.”
(McKennon v. Nashville Banner Pub. Co. (1995) 513 U.S. 352, 362–363.) The burden is on the
employer to prove not only that it could have fired an employee for the later-discovered
misconduct, but that it would in fact have done so. (O’Day v. McDonnell Douglas Helicopter Co.
(9th Cir. 1996) 79 F.3d 756, 759.) The employer must show that such a firing would have taken
place as a matter of “settled company policy.” (Murillo v. Rite Stuff Foods, Inc. (1998) 65
Cal.App.4th 833, 846.)
Target states that on Plaintiff’s application for employment with Target, Plaintiff made
affirmative representations about her job experience, skills, and expertise as a store manager for
BBW and PBO. (DuCharme Decl., ¶¶ 2-3, Exhs. A-B.) However, Target believes that many of
those representations were false because Plaintiff’s performance at Target was not consistent with
her representations. (DuCharme Decl., ¶ 5, Exh. D.) Target also asserts that Plaintiff told a
coworker that she had sued her previous employer and claimed she would sue Target. Furthermore,
Target argues that Plaintiff has waived her privacy rights to those records because Plaintiff had
signed an Acknowledgment and Authorization regarding a Background Check Disclosure,
acknowledging and agreed that Target could request her background information. (DuCharme
Decl. ¶ 4, Ex. C.) Given this, Target argues that it is entitled to discover information related to
Plaintiff’s training, job duties, performance, and misconduct at her prior jobs.
On reply, Plaintiff argues that any allegation of Plaintiff’s misconduct can be found in
Target’s own records. Plaintiff also argues that any misrepresentations to her own job experience
cannot be established by her prior employment records, but does not explain how this conclusion
was reached. Plaintiff also points out that Target had an opportunity to conduct a background check
before retaining Plaintiff, and that their lack of diligence in doing so makes their arguments
baseless.

When the arguments are considered, Plaintiff’s arguments that the Subpoenas constitute a
professional death sentence are overblown. Here, any negative stigma created by the Subpoenas
would have already been completely rendered upon service of the Subpoenas. Furthermore,
Target’s argument that Plaintiff’s written authorization to allow Target to conduct a background
check on Plaintiff would constitute a wholesale waiver of any right to privacy into Plaintiff’s
employment history is unpersuasive. If such were the case, every applicant to a job opening who
signs such a waiver would lose any privacy rights in any future litigation. In general, “[t]he waiver
of an important right must be a voluntary and knowing act done with sufficient awareness of the
relevant circumstances and likely consequences.” (County of Riverside v. Superior Court (2002)
27 Cal.4th 793, 806, emphasis in original.)
Nonetheless, Plaintiff does maintain a privacy interest in his personnel files. However,
Target’s right to pursue its after-acquired evidence defense outweighs the privacy interest to some
extent. If Plaintiff was terminated from her prior employment rather than leaving for a “better
opportunity,” then Target may be justified in refusing to hire Plaintiff in the first instance or in
later terminating Plaintiff if that information later came to light.
Moreover, in the parties’ meet and confer correspondences, Plaintiff appears to concede
that Target is entitled to discover information related to Plaintiff’s prior job applications to BWE
and PBO, her employment agreements showing Plaintiff’s prior pay rate and other benefits, and
the job description of Plaintiff’s prior positions at BWE and PBO. (See Davtyan Decl. iso iso
BBW/PBO Motion, Exh. 2.) Nonetheless, Plaintiff is correct in arguing that the Subpoenas are
overbroad to the extent it seeks interview records, all compensation records, and
separation/severance agreements.

Ruling
Given this, the Court GRANTS the Motion, IN PART, and quash the portion of the
Subpoenas seeking those documents. The Subpoenas are the most reasonable way to obtain this
information, and Plaintiff provides no support demonstrating that this evidence is not relevant to
Target’s affirmative defenses. For clarity, the scope of the Subpoenas are modified as follows:
1. All job applications completed by Plaintiff;
2. All resumes, cover letters, and other documents submitted by Plaintiff in seeking
employment with BWE or PBO;
3. All interview notes, summaries, and other documents describing the information
discussed during Plaintiff’s job interview(s) for employment with BWE or PBO;
4. All offer letters, employment agreements/contracts, and other documents showing
Plaintiff’s pay rate and entitlement to employee benefits;
5. The job description for each position Plaintiff held during her employment with BWE
or PBO;
6. Any and all documents regarding Plaintiff’s job duties during her employment with
BWE or PBO;
7. Any and all documents regarding Plaintiff’s performance during her employment with
BWE or PBO;
8. All disciplinary records for misconduct relating to Plaintiff;
9. Any and all documents regarding any complaints Plaintiff made during her
employment with BWE or PBO;
10. All documents reflecting compensation paid to Plaintiff;
11. If applicable, all documents related to the end of Plaintiff’s employment, including but
not limited to documents showing the reason Plaintiff’s employment ended, separation
agreements, severance agreements, resignation letter(s), exit interview notes, and final
pay records; and
12. Any non-privileged documents related to any litigation brought by Plaintiff against
BBW that are not available in the public record, including Plaintiff’s deposition
transcript, discovery responses, document productions, and the like.
D. Sanctions
Here, Plaintiff requests sanctions in the sum of $5,250 for successfully bringing each
Motion (Davtyan Decl. iso BBW/PBO Motion, ¶¶ 4-7), while Target requests sanctions in the sum
of $6,900.00 for successfully opposing the BBW Motion (DuCharme Decl iso BBW Motion, ¶ 15)
and the sum of $3,450.00 for successfully opposing the PBO Motion (DuCharme Decl. iso PBO
Motion, ¶ 11).

The Court DENIES both parties’ request for sanctions. Here, each side should bear their
own fees and costs because both parties won some and also lost some. Furthermore, although
meeting and conferring is not a pre-requisite to bringing the Motions, it appears that both parties
failed to meet and confer in good faith before the Motions were brought by Plaintiff.
Movant to give Notice and prepare Order.

Dated:

Judge Gilbert G. Ochoa
